en: The Śivopaniṣad [describes] the Lord Śrī Mahākāla, who sits upon the peak of Kailāsa, worshipped by all the immortals,
the destroyer of time, and one who has reached the further shore of knowledge.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites with devotion, the great sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, being well-restrained, questioned him for the sake of the welfare of all living beings. (1.2)
O Blessed One, how can those men of dull intellect who do not find the yoga of knowledge be liberated from the terrible ocean of existence? 1.3
Thus questioned by the wise Rishi Ātreya, the serene-souled Mahākāla spoke for the sake of liberating those of dull intellect. 1.4.
Mahādeva said: In former times, the eternal Śiva-dharmas were proclaimed by Rudra to the Goddess and all the Gaṇas in summary form, comprising tens of millions of verses.
Having carefully observed here the lifespan, wisdom, and power of men, as well as their affliction by the threefold suffering and the delusion caused by the thirst for enjoyment. (1.6)
Those dharmas were taught by Skanda, Nandin, and other supreme sages,
having extracted the essence [of the teachings] through various correct treatises.
I shall proclaim the Śivopaniṣad, the supreme essence even among essences, which is brief in its text yet vast in its meaning, for the welfare of the world.
Those who repeatedly utter "Śiva, Śiva" and this primordial name "Śānta" with devotion are themselves Śivas; of this there is no doubt. (1.9)
All conscious beings are inauspicious and bound by fetters;
because He is distinct from them, the Lord is remembered as Śiva. 1.10

The qualities (guṇa), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs (indriya), and the gross elements (bhūta)—these twenty-four are proclaimed to be the fetters (pāśa). 1.11.
The twenty-fifth is the innate ignorance of all embodied beings;
it is the root of the net of bonds, and for us, it is primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as the cause.
In the absence of knowledge of reality, persons are bound by the fetters of bondage;
but through my nature, the wise are liberated from the cage of fetters. 1.13
In the Śiva-āgama, the Puruṣa is the twenty-sixth, an ignorant creature;
the twenty-seventh is declared to be Śiva, the Lord of the entire universe. (1.14)
Because Śiva is perfectly complete, omniscient, all-pervading, and the Lord, therefore he is the remover of bonds; he is pure by his very nature.
Supreme over the bonds of the individual soul, peaceful, the teacher of supreme knowledge—by recognizing Śiva, who exists for the welfare of all beings, one is liberated. 1.16.
This alone is the supreme knowledge: the two syllables "Śi-va.
Through inquiry, they expand like a drop of oil upon water. (1.17)
By whomsoever these two syllables, "Śi-va," are uttered even once, the girdle has been fastened by him for the sake of attaining liberation. (1.18)
This two-syllabled Śiva-mantra is recorded in the Śivopaniṣad;
furthermore, this one-syllabled mantra is established as simply "Om. (1.19)
Since one is swiftly liberated from all sins merely by the recitation of the name of Śiva, this supreme mantra consists of two syllables. 1.20.
He who constantly practices this two-syllable mantra, "Śiva, Śiva," or even the single syllable, goes to the supreme state. (1.21)
One should give a name of an auspicious nature to friends, kinsmen, and relatives;
by even chanting that [name], one becomes freed from sin and goes to the city of Śiva.
That man who is permeated by that state should be known as Śiva, peaceful;
he remains forever free from anxiety and is liberated at the end of the body.
The heart is to be known as the internal organ, the supreme abode of Śiva;
the lotus of the heart is the altar there, and the *liṅga* is held to be the syllable *oṃ*. (1.24)
The person should be known as the establisher; truth is remembered as the sweeping;
non-violence is declared to be the cow-dung; and supreme peace is the water. (1.25)
The wise one should perform sweeping; dispassion is considered the sandalwood paste.
One should worship through the yoga of meditation with the white flowers of contentment. (1.26)

Incense made from guggulu arising from breath control (prāṇāyāma) should be offered; withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) is the food offering (naivedya), and non-stealing is the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa). 1.27.
Thus, having worshipped the supreme Śiva with divine offerings, one who is free from all attachments should recite [the mantra] and meditate for the sake of liberation. 1.28.
Released from the yoga of knowledge and fully engaged in the yoga of action,
he shall go to the city of Śiva upon death by virtue of that auspicious karma.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there, at the dissolution of all embodied beings,
one shall attain the knowledge of Śiva through the dharma of Śiva and thereby obtain liberation.
Those who practice the yoga of knowledge are liberated immediately upon the fall of the body;
those who practice the yoga of action, having experienced their enjoyments, are liberated at the time of cosmic dissolution.
Therefore, through the yoga of those who know wisdom, as well as through the yoga of action for those who do not so know—
all those men who have taken refuge in Śiva are liberated.
Those whose karma is stainless for the sake of the knowledge of Śiva, having attained enjoyments, are liberated at the time of dissolution through that very knowledge of Śiva. (1.33)
Indeed, those for whom no karma exists must have their knowledge proclaimed; they are liberated without returning as long as that karma does not come to be. (1.34)
Therefore, one should worship with all available resources the guru who knows the knowledge of Śiva;
and one should bestow the gift of the Vidyā out of a desire to attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1.35)
The Śiva-yogin, the knower of Śiva, the reciter of Śiva’s name, the one preeminent in austerity, and the karma-yogin in due order—these five are the recipients of liberation. // 1.36 //
I shall briefly state that which is the root of the yoga of action: the characteristic mark and the abode; therein action proceeds. (1.37)
Thus ends the first chapter, the Exposition of Liberation, in the Śivopaniṣad.
Now, the embryo previously situated within the *liṅga* should be tripled;
or else, having divided it from the embryo, one should install the *liṅga* in the temple of Śiva.
The width of the altar should be equal to the length of the linga;
the height of the altar should be one-third of the linga.
One part should be placed upon the ground, the second in the middle of the altar, and the worship should be performed in the third part; thus the Liṅga is established in three ways. (2.3)

The square [mandala] is situated on the ground; from its center, an eight-sided [shape] is formed for the altar, and for the purpose of worship, a circle should be made with a width three times its length.
Skanda is situated in the lower part, and the Goddess is situated in the middle;
above them is Rudra, or alternatively, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara in succession.
These indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three qualities (guṇas);
these indeed are the three Vedas; and this other [universe] is likewise established in a threefold manner.
Nine cubits is known as the largest [liṅga], six cubits is the medium, and one should know that three cubits is the smallest; this is the traditional measurement of the liṅga. (2.7)

The width [of the temple] should not be less than the length of the inner sanctum (garbha), nor should it be recommended if it exceeds that; it should be established as being equal to or greater than the width of the inner sanctum. (2.8)
The illustrious one should fashion the palace and then divide it again into three parts:
one part shall be the base (jaṅghā), and two parts are known as the floral ornament (mañjarī).
One should fashion the śukanāsa (front porch) occupying half the portion of the mañjarī;
its width and length should be half of the inner sanctum (garbha), making it very beautiful.
One should fashion the *śukanāsa* (front porch) at one-third of the *garbha* (inner sanctum);
it is half as wide as the *garbha* and twice as long as the *garbha*.
The legs should be made with a heap of fingers [measuring] one cluster of blossoms;
the pavilion to its left should be known as half the size of the temple.

The platform (jagatī) extending one-fourth the width of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) shall be raised to that same height; the courtyard (aṅgaṇa), together with the platform, shall be proportioned according to the dimensions of the palace (prāsāda).
One should construct a rampart all around it, adorned with watchtowers and gates, and within the enclosure of that rampart, one should erect a lofty site for the bull.
Nandīśvara and Mahākāla are stationed at the two door-posts;
to the south of the enclosure wall, one should construct [the hall] provided with all necessary implements.
The great abode of the lords of yogis should be made five stories or three stories high,
protected by a wall, and provided with a place for the Maitra ritual.
Ten units from that site, provided with auspicious trees and water, lies the kitchen to the southeast;
to the east of that is the sacrificial pavilion.
The abode of Caṇḍeśa is in the northeast, the flower garden likewise in the north;
the storehouse is in the northwest, and the abode of Varuṇa is in the west.
One should establish a site for the weapon-shed in the southwest, containing *śamī* wood and *kuśa* grass, situated within the city for the benefit of all the world. (2.19)
In a secluded forest, at the glorious abode of Śambhu,
as many atoms as there are within the temple of Śiva, so many yogins gathered together.
For as many Manvantaras as there are [liṅgas], the agent enjoys rewards in the city of Śiva;
[therein are found] great, peerless liṅgas and vast sanctuaries.
Having performed this, the virtuous man obtains great enjoyments and, in the end, eternal liberation;
he should perform the consecration of the Liṅga when its proper characteristics are present.
Having purified with the five products of the cow and having performed worship,
one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) using leaves of the *pālāśa*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha* trees, along with speckled butter, sesame seeds, and barley.
One should perform the fire-rite and offer three full oblations;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations to Śiva, the wise practitioner should touch the base of the liṅga.

Thus, in the middle and at the end, one should fashion the eight Lords of the Embodiments (mūrtīśvaras) within the embodiments using their respective form-mantras; the ninth is traditionally held to be the installer (sthāpaka).
In the morning, one should install the liṅga with the nine mantras in sequence;
having performed the great bathing and worship, and having installed the liṅga, one should worship it thoroughly.
One should give the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those who bear the form of the Guru,
and one should give the middle sacrificial fee to all the ascetics (yatis).

And for the sake of the wretched, the blind, and the miserable, he should provide all kinds of food, including all types of edibles, grains, drinks, and the like, as well as any food that is not forbidden. (2.28)
One should prepare offerings for those who have arrived and present a bali-offering to the spirits;
specifically at night, one should give a bali-offering to the hosts of Mothers.
Now hear the fruit of merit for one who installs a *liṅga* in this manner: having delivered thirty generations of his lineage, he shall be surrounded by servants. (2.30)
Accompanied by his wife, sons, friends, and all his kinsmen,
a man shall leave behind the mire of sin and go to the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed great pleasures there, he shall attain liberation at the time of universal dissolution.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Abode of the Liṅga," in the Śivopaniṣad.
Then, by other kings who possess little wealth but are devoted to Śiva,
two houses for Śiva’s peace-offerings should be constructed within their own hermitages according to their capacity.
In the northeast quarter of the house, or even to the north, one should dig the ground,
lift up the earth, and carefully remove all embedded objects.
A temple for Śiva should be constructed measuring eight cubits;
one should fashion it so that it is slightly longer on the southern and northern sides.
And one should attach four firm cloths, each measuring one cubit in size, to the four corners to serve as supports for the arghya vessel and other items. (3.4)
In the middle of the womb, one should fashion a very beautiful Śiva-altar,
slightly raised toward the north and provided with four corners.
Three cubits in length and breadth, and sixteen finger-breadths in height; its heads [should be] half a cubit in both length and width. (3.6)
One should prepare this "Śiva-altar," measuring four cubits and level at its top, for the purpose of arranging the image, the food offering, and the lamp. (3.7)
The rite should be performed with a Śiva-linga, or with a jewel, a rosary, or an earthen image;
and upon half of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), they construct another altar that is circular.
One should not keep in the house a stone linga sixteen finger-breadths in height and twice that in width; rather, one should worship a linga made of gemstone.
One should perform the worship of the earthly linga at the three junctions of the day, or alternatively, another [linga] day by day;
for all castes, the crystal linga grants all desires.
One who is completely free from all faults will otherwise incur fault; such a person shall be long-lived, strong, illustrious, possessed of sons, wealthy, and happy. (3.11)
By worshipping an earthen liṅga, one obtains a desired boon;
therefore, indeed, the earthen liṅga should be known as the accomplisher of all goals. (3.12)
The wise person should constantly worship that which is faultless and easily obtained;
for as great as the liṅga is, and as great as the faith in the worship, [so shall be the result]. (3.13)
In that same manner, great merit should be understood according to the corresponding proportions.
As many atoms as there are in the image, the linga, and the altar, for so many kalpas shall the maker of those [objects] enjoy great wealth in the city of Śiva.
Thus ends the third chapter, "The Abode of Śiva," in the Śivopaniṣad.
Now, in front [of the main hall], there shall be a single, undivided, and uninterrupted peace-pavilion (śāntimaṇḍapa),
measuring eight cubits from east to west and twelve from north to south.
Having placed two cloths connected to the door and walls and covered with *kapicchu* and *śuka* grass, they should serve as a screen for the *sruva* ladle and other implements.
The door in the temple of Śiva should be known as having three branches (triśākha), ninety finger-breadths in height, and half of that in width, provided with a good door-leaf. 4.3.
Long, measuring ninety-five [units] and beautifully adorned with five branches, it was a magnificent carriage-pavilion provided with two excellent door-panels. (4.4)
The door should be known as facing west, which accomplishes all purposes;
in its absence, it should face east, but never toward the north or the south. (4.5)
Two very beautiful windows should be made on the southern and northern walls for the purpose of letting out smoke. (4.6)
Lattice windows should be constructed all around the southern portion;
it should be provided with an upper turret that has a slightly perforated covering.
The sacrificial pit for the Śiva-agnihotra is circular, measuring one cubit in size; it has a beautiful square altar adorned with three girdles (mekhalās). // 4.8 //
A wall two cubits wide and five cubits high should be constructed as a most beautiful shelter for the Śiva-agnihotra.
One should fashion the seven elements, beginning with the ground, the pillars, and the plinth,
free from the application of binding joints, with equal intervals between their positions.
One should diligently construct a great temple for the fire of Śiva out of bricks,
provided with four necks or else with a single neck. (4.11)
The sanctuary of Śiva’s Agnihotra should be plastered with lime and adorned with five *aṇḍakas*, and it should be provided with four *aṇḍakas*.
Outside, that very same area is the *jagatī*, three cubits in height, well-paved, and of the same width, adorned with girdles and other ornaments. (4.13)
And here a *jagatī* should be constructed; beneath it, on all sides, it should be two cubits in width and half of that [width] again in height.
Another very beautiful Rudra-altar (rudravedī) should be constructed, measuring ten cubits in extent and four finger-breadths in height. 4.15.
One should always offer a perpetual oblation (*nityabali*) to Rudra, the groups of Mothers, and the Lords of the Quarters, accompanied by the first portion of all cooked food.
Another altar for all beings should be constructed outside, measuring two cubits;
and a place for the bull should be made facing the gaze of Śiva.
The space of the foremost Ṛṣi-savitar is the bull (vṛṣa) to be constructed in the west;
and below that space, there should be the triple-chambered altar for the libation to the ancestors.
One should cause it to be constructed with a wall both inside and out, adorned with a magnificent gopura,
and provided with flower gardens and water up to the edge of the wall.
A wise person should construct a temple of Śiva made of clay or wood and thatched with grass; by the arrangement of two levels of ground, he should cause it to be raised up.
To the south of Śiva, one should construct a dwelling suitable for his enjoyment,
provided with beds and seats, and built according to the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā).
The banner, the lion, the bull, and the elephant—these four are remembered as auspicious;
whereas smoke, the horse, the donkey, and the crow—these four cause the destruction of wealth.
Having multiplied the length and width of the house by three from the beginning, one should divide it by eight; the remainder shall indicate the house.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who, having thus prepared a house of peace, should devoutly maintain the fire of Rudra for even a single day. (4.24)
Surrounded by his wife, sons, friends, and servants, he shall deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage and attain the world of the gods. (4.25)
Others were beautiful women of golden complexion, lovely to behold, with dark complexions like the petals of a blue lotus and full, rounded breasts. 4.26.
Together with them, he sports at will in celestial palaces of great enjoyment that fulfill all desires, for as long as the dissolution of the world lasts.

Then, seeing [the world] being consumed by the fire at the end of the aeon and becoming utterly distraught, one becomes even more dispassionate toward the great ocean of worldly existence and its enjoyments.
Then he should inquire of the Rudras stationed there who have reached the further shore of knowledge;
having obtained from them the knowledge of Śiva, he shall attain peaceful nirvāṇa. (4.29)
And if he is not dispassionate toward enjoyments, he is born for seven lifetimes as a glorious lord of the earth, or, by his own will, as an excellent twice-born man.
At the end of the seventh birth, one shall attain the knowledge of Śiva;
through that knowledge, detached from saṃsāra and purified, one presides over the voids.
Thus, this entire range of activities and their fruits has been stated in brief;
now, furthermore, we shall describe the fruit arising from each individual substance in the context of the festival.
Having offered into the fire a single pill of excellent fragrance, lac devoid of animal parts, and [lac] the size of a cotton seed, one shall hear the result. (4.33)
For as many times as fragrant pills are offered into the auspicious fire by way of number, for that many tens of millions of years one enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva.
Having offered an oblation of sandalwood into the fire with a measure of one finger-breadth,
one shall dwell in the city of Śiva for two hundred million years, enjoying divine pleasures.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are filaments in the flower offered into the fire, for that long one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The *nāgakesara* flower is said to be equal to half a portion of saffron;
the fruit that was prescribed for sandalwood applies to *uśīra* at half that amount.

Whatever merit is said to arise from worshipping the auspicious signs with flowers, incense, food offerings, curd, milk, ghee, and so forth, that which arises from the fire oblation (homa) is ten times greater. 4.38.
Having offered three fuel-sticks into the fire with the names of Śiva,
Umā, and Skanda, one should afterwards offer oblations of sesame seeds and cooked rice in the proper sequence.

Having offered auspicious fuel-sticks made from the sprouts of the *palāśa* tree, which have been consecrated with *ariṣṭa* and sprinkled with clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*), hear what fruit one shall obtain. 4.40.
For as many times as there are palāśa sprouts offered into the fire,
for that many kalpas one is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments.
Having offered auspicious fuel-sticks into the fire produced from the center of that target,
he enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva for a period of time equal to half a kalpa.
One should offer fuel-sticks and fruits of the *śamī* tree for a hundred thousand years;
the remaining fuel-sticks produced from milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) are to be treated like half-fruits of the *śamī*.
Having offered sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter, equal in number to the grains of sesame [in a standard measure],
he enjoys pleasures for as many hundreds of thousands of years in the city of Śiva.
As long as one is ignorant of the divine medicinal herbs, the fruit is said to be equal to that of ordinary sesame;
however, for black sesame seeds compared to other types, the fruit is double. (4.45)
Parched grain and unbroken rice together with wheat bestow the fruit of a hundred thousand years; those of the remaining species of seeds should be known as yielding ten thousand years. (4.46)
In a fire produced from *palāśa* fuel, the fruit of the oblation is doubled;
in a fire enriched by milky trees, the fruit shall be one and a half times greater. (4.47)
If the sacrificial rite is performed when the fire is not kindled or when it is smoky, it is fruitless;
likewise, the one being born would be blind and afflicted by poverty. (4.48)
One should not kindle the fire with thorny trees and perform the oblation; rather, one should enkindle the fire with dry, fresh, and commendable wood. 4.49.
Having thus offered the oblation of clarified butter, one shall attain the world of Śiva;
there, for a hundred kalpas, one enjoys divine pleasures according to one's desire.
When the *sruk* ladle has been placed [upon the fire] and the vow has been fulfilled,
the oblation that is offered into the fire is called the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Having offered one final full oblation, purified by Śiva through Śiva,
he attains all desires and is established in the world of Śiva.
Surrounded by his servants and accompanied by those born of all the [divine] lineages,
he enjoys his desired pleasures until the dissolution of the world.
And then, when the dissolution has arrived, having attained supreme knowledge through the grace of the Lord alone, one is liberated from the ocean of existence.
Even that man who merely witnesses the *śivapūrṇāhuti* falling into the fire is liberated from all sins and shall go to the city of Śiva. (4.55)
All living beings, both moving and stationary, who are touched by the smoke of the Śiva-fire are liberated from sin and go to heaven; of this there is no doubt. (4.56)
Whether they exist or do not exist, all living beings— both mobile and immobile— who are born upon the great altar of the sacrifice to Śiva, go to the abode of Śiva.
In the absence of ghee, one should prepare the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with milk or oil;
a person may offer linseed oil in the absence of sesame oil.
[The paste] produced from mustard, *iṅguda*, mango, *karañja*, and *madhuka*;
and that arising from *priyaṅgu*, *bilva*, *pippalī*, and coconut. (4.59)
In the absence of clarified butter (ājya), one should prepare oil in this manner and other such ways;
sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) are prescribed as being made from dūrvā grass or bilva leaves. 4.60.
For the sake of rice, one should offer milk, curd, or roots and fruits;
for the sake of sesame seeds, one should use rice grains; and for the sake of darbha grass, one should use green blades of grass. (4.61)
In the absence of enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), one should fashion them from reeds or bamboo;
in the absence of firewood, one should kindle the fire with grass and cow dung. (4.62)
In the absence of cow dung, one should perform the oblation in a large body of water; if water is unavailable, the oblation should be performed on a pleasing plot of ground. (4.63)
One should offer the oblation into the right hand of a Brahmin, or into an *aśvattha* tree in his absence; for a goat, one should offer it into its right ear or at the root of *kuśa* grass. (4.64)

The wise one should offer oblations into the fire of his own self when all other fires are unavailable; established in the rule of the yoga of action, he should not abandon the rite even in the absence [of external materials]. (4.65)
Even in times of adversity, whoever performs mental worship of the Śiva-fire shall cast off the veil of delusion and attain supreme peace. (4.66)
The supreme Śiva-yogins perform the Prāṇāgnihotra;
they are liberated from external rituals and are fully absorbed in knowledge and meditation. (4.67)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, concerning the Peace Chamber and the Fire Ritual, in the Śivopaniṣad.
Now follows the great Agneya bath, which destroys misfortune and impurity, removes all sins, is divine, and increases ascetic merit, prosperity, and fame. (5.1)
By Rudra in the form of fire, his own supreme splendor and power—pure, in the form of prosperity, and the remover of misfortune—was emitted. (5.2)
This mantra-consecrated destroyer of yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and piśācas is for the protection of children and in the houses of women who have recently given birth.
And that twice-born man who, having performed the three-fold covering of the food, eats even when seated in the row of a Śūdra, is not defiled by the faults of the row. (5.4)
If food has been half-eaten or is defiled by insects, hair, and the like, it becomes pure once that portion has been removed and touched by earth. (5.5)
Cow-dung from the forest or dried cow-manure is recommended;
it should be free of gravel and dust, or in their absence, one may use wood-ash.
From the creepers of their own domestic hermitages, by means of the ashes from the potter’s workshop, when the cow-dung and the bricks have been burnt. (5.7)

Ash is found everywhere; it should be taken from a place devoid of living beings, appearing as white as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and used for the protection against the acquisition of suffering. (5.8)
One should carefully collect the ashes and protect them with diligence, so that they are not defiled by cats, mice, or other such creatures. (5.9)
Śiva-ash is proclaimed to be that which is free from the five defects, endowed with the five qualities, and consecrated by reciting the Śivaikādaśikā mantra.
And the fifth [type] is corrupted by birth, craft, speech, body, or place;
it destroys evil, belongs to Śaṅkara, is a protection and a purifier, bestows yoga, and possesses [these] qualities. // 5.11 //
Because it illuminates the auspicious and peaceful observance of Śiva, and because it consumes all sins, it is celebrated as "bhasma" (ashes). 5.12.
The ash-bath, the bath of Śiva, is remembered as superior to the Varuṇa-bath;
it is free from living organisms and moss, and like fire, it is devoid of mud.
Water that has not been drawn previously during the night becomes impure, even if it comes from rivers, ponds, wells, or mountain springs. (5.14)
The Vāruṇa bath is declared to be common to all embodied beings;
however, the ash-bath is said to be the uncommon one for the twice-born.
From bathing with water three times a day, ill health arises;
whereas the fire-based bath pacifies disease and fulfills all desires. (5.16)

One who is fit for Śiva should perform ritual bathing at the three junctions of the day, at midnight, after eating, after vomiting food, and during such acts as the excretion of feces and urine. (5.17)
On a level patch of ground strewn with ashes and devoid of living creatures,
the yogi, meditating upon Śiva, should lie down at the end of the night.
The destination attained even by one who sleeps on ashes after staying there for a single night cannot be reached by a householder, even through hundreds of sacrifices.
A householder should perform his bath with the *tryāyuṣa* mantras and apply the *tripuṇḍra* marks;
an ascetic, however, should perform a full-body bath from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.

A Śiva-devotee, whether a Śūdra or one living in the household stage of life, should apply [the ashes] on the heart, the head, and the forehead; thus he becomes known in the three worlds and obtains the fruit of the ash-bath. 5.21.
The peaceful Gaṇas who have gone forth have attained prosperity in five ways;
by applying ashes to the head, forehead, heart, and both arms, one obtains the fruit of the ash-bath.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who performs the bath with ashes for a year, or half a year, or on the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight. (5.23)
For as many thousands of years as there are atoms gathered in the sacred ash of Śiva, for that long one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage, accompanied by his wife, sons, and others, and surrounded by all his friends, kinsmen, and servants. (5.25)
Having enjoyed there great pleasures according to his desire— pleasures that fulfill all wishes—
and having attained the yoga of knowledge, he shall obtain liberation at the time of universal dissolution.
By him who has taken up the ultimate vow ending in ashes, Rudra indeed wanders upon the earth in this very body. (5.27)
Those men who, day after day, bow down to one who is peaceful and devoted to the ash-bath,
become liberated from all sins and go to the city of Śiva.
This is the supreme ablution, pertaining to fire and fashioned by Śiva; one who performs it daily at the three junctions of the day while reciting [mantras] shall attain yoga. 5.29
He who gives ashes for the purpose of bathing to a Śiva-yogin shall enjoy pleasures in the city of Śiva for a kalpa, and at the end, become the best of the twice-born. (5.30)
The fire-related, the water-related, the mantra-related, the wind-related, and the Indra-related as the fifth;
the mental, the water for pacification, and likewise the knowledge-bath as the eighth. (5.31)
The unsurpassed fire-bath (āgneyasnāna) should be performed with the Rudra-mantra;
or the water-bath (vāruṇasnāna) should be performed by one who has assumed the form of Varuṇa.
Placing one's hand upon the crown of the head, one should recite the Śiva-ekādaśikā while meditating on the peaceful Śiva; this is remembered as the supreme mantra-bath.
One should perform the Vāyavya bath with the mantra whose essence is the wind, using the dust raised by the wind kicked up from the hooves of cows. 5.34.

When the sun is cloudless and it rains, one should perform a bath while standing in the eastern direction; using the mantra of the Sky-form, that is proclaimed as the rite dedicated to Indra (aindra). 5.35.
Taking water in the hand, one should call to mind all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and sprinkle it upon one's head; this is called the mental bath (mānasa-snāna). 5.36.
Whatever merit is gained by bathing in all the sacred fords, lakes, and shrines upon the earth—that merit is obtained through the water of patience. (5.37)
A person is not purified by sacred fords, nor by austerities, nor by great sacrifices, nor by all manner of gifts, as one is purified by patience. (5.38)
Therefore, whether reviled, beaten, insulted, or treated with contempt, one should practice patience toward those who are intolerant, out of a desire to win heaven and liberation. (5.39)
That very attainment which belongs to the knowers of Brahman, that very attainment which belongs to the ascetics,
and that very goal which belongs to those devoted to yoga— that same state belongs to those who possess forgiveness.
The sage who has always bathed in the stainless waters of knowledge should be known as pure, spotless, and perfectly purified, like the rays of the sun. (5.41)
Just as the sap of the pure and the impure does not stain a calf even without hands, so too the wise one, being perfectly stainless, is not tainted by defects. (5.42)
Having bathed in any one of these, one with a pure disposition shall go to Śiva;
even one who has bathed but possesses an impure disposition may obtain the fruit by performing worship.
Water, sacred mantras, compassion, charity, truthfulness, restraint of the senses, knowledge, and purity of being—these are declared to be the eightfold purification. (5.44)
And at the base of the palm of the thumb is situated the Brāhma-tīrtha;
having sipped water with that, one becomes pure when permeated by the Śiva-mantra. (5.45)
That which is below the maiden's [thumb] is called the divine *tīrtha*;
the *tīrtha* at the base of the forefinger is the ancestral (*pitrya*), for the performance of rites for the ancestors. (5.46)
The sacred ford (tīrtha) called Āriṣa is said to be in the middle of the middle fingers;
however, the Śiva-tīrtha is established in the center of the hollow of the hand.
On the palm of the left hand, the sacred bathing place named Auma is proclaimed;
through its union with the Śivomā-tīrtha, one should perform the ritual bath and consecration. (5.48)

A wise man, always wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī), should satisfy the gods with water drawn from the divine part of the hand (daiva-tīrtha) by lifting his right hand. 5.49.
The libation for the ancestors should be performed with water mixed with sesame seeds while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī);
the libation for all beings should be performed with water alone while wearing the thread around the neck (nivītī).
When the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder, it is called *upavīta*;
when worn over the right shoulder, it is *prācīnāvīta*; and when it remains around the neck, it is *nivīta*. (5.51)
Having performed the libation for the ancestors, one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun;
then, having approached the Sun, one should worship Śiva immediately thereafter. (5.52)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on the bathing with Śiva-ashes, in the Śivopaniṣad.
Then, having worshipped Śiva with devotion, one should prepare an offering of food;
whatever food one eats oneself, that one should present before him. 6.1.
He who, having prepared various kinds of food and delicacies with great care,
should offer them to Śiva, shall rejoice in the world of Śiva for ten million kalpas.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who gives a ripe *śrīphala* to Śiva, or offers it as an oblation to the Guru. (6.3)
In the city of Śiva, he enjoys pleasures with glorious great vehicles for more than ten thousand years; at the end of that time, he becomes a Lord of Fortune (Śrīpati).
He who offers a single ripe wood-apple to the Lord is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for a hundred thousand years. (6.5)
Whoever offers a single ripe mango fruit to Śambhu shall sport with enjoyments for ten million years in the city of Śiva.
Whoever offers a single ripe vaṭa fruit to Śiva is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for a hundred thousand years.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who offers a single ripe, fully blossomed, fresh pomegranate to Śiva or to the Guru. (6.8)
For as many times as the number of those seeds is proclaimed auspiciously,
for that many eighty thousand years he is highly honored in the world of Śiva.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who, with devotion, offers ripe grapes to Śiva or to the yogis of Śiva. (6.10)
As long as the enumeration of those fruits is proclaimed for both,
for so many thousands of yugas is one honored in the world of Rudra.
Whatever merit there is in grapes, that same merit is found in dates, as well as in royal trees and *pārāvata* fruits. (6.12)
He who offers a ripe orange to Maheśvara sports with great enjoyments in the city of Śiva for eight hundred thousand [years].
Whatever merit is found in *bījapūra* fruits, half of that is in *likuca* fruits, and half of that again is in *jambū* fruits; the same merit is also found in *tinduka* fruits. (6.14)
One should offer a jackfruit or a coconut to Śiva;
for a hundred thousand years, one is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments.
The *puruṣa* tree, the *priyāla*, the flowers of the *madhūka*,
ripe *jambū* fruits, and the fruits of the *vaikaṅkata*.
Having offered each and every fruit with devotion to Śarva,
one is honored in the world of Rudra for ten thousand years.
He who offers a ripe *kṣīrikā* fruit to Śiva rejoices with great enjoyments in the city of Śiva for a hundred thousand years.
Whoever should offer fruits such as vālukā and trapusa, or even ripe karamardaka, to Śiva or to the Guru; 6.19.
For ten thousand years he is honored in the world of Rudra [by offering] well-ripened jujubes and tamarind fruits.
Indeed, the ripe fruits of the *āmalaka* tree are beautiful to behold;
likewise, there are other such vegetables, roots, and fruits.
He offers them to Śarva; hear what fruit he shall obtain:
in each individual fruit, he shall attain enjoyments in successive order. (6.22)
For five thousand years, one is honored in the world of Rudra; likewise for well-prepared wheat, rice, and so forth, as well as roasted barley flour. (6.23)
One should offer it to Śarva; hear now the meritorious fruit thereof:
as many seeds as one offers, even if they have been broken, so much auspicious merit shall accrue.
He who offers cooked stalks of sugarcane to Śiva is glorified in the world of Rudra for as many thousands of years.
Or if one gives it with devotion to the Guru, hear now the fruit of that merit:
for each stalk and leaf, he rejoices in the world of Varuṇa for a year. (6.26)
Having offered to the Supreme Lord even a mere drop of juice [of the size of] a pearl-oyster shell, one receives fivefold the fruit of Pauṇḍraka, together with enjoyments in the City of Śiva.
Having offered pure molasses to Śiva or to the Guru, one is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for ten million years. (6.28)
A human being who offers a single fruit of jaggery to Śiva obtains a reward a thousand times greater than that of sugarcane juice. (6.29)
In the auspicious world of Ambakoṭi, one rejoices with great enjoyments;
the fruit of an offering of sugar-candy is a hundred times greater than that of an offering of jaggery.
When offering sugar, one should present a thousand times more than the amount of candied sugar;
one should offer pure, great granulated sugar to Śaṅkara.
A person is honored in the world of Śiva for more than ten million kalpas by offering clarified butter that is pure, fried, prepared, and well-consecrated. (6.32)
Listen to what fruit one obtains by offering [this] for a month to Śarva:
the merit that is proclaimed as resulting from the gift of all fruits without exception. (6.33)
One shall obtain all that merit by the offering of great gifts,
as well as divine jackfruits that are delicious and fragrant.
One should offer it to Śarva; hear now the fruit of that merit:
for more than ten million kalpas, the man remains established in the world of Śiva.
He who daily partakes of water purified by a cloth shall rejoice with great enjoyments, drinking the divine nectar of Śiva. (6.36)

Listen to the fruit of the merit of that person who, for the sake of the happiness of the devotees of Śiva, constructs great lakes; he would obtain the merit [equivalent to] being in the presence of Śiva. (6.37)
Having obtained all that merit, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
whatever food, drink, fruit, or other such thing is desired by oneself—6.38.
Whatever one desires as the highest enjoyment should be offered to Śiva;
yet Śiva, because of his perfection, does not consume anything belonging to anyone. (6.39)
However, having made everything resemble God, it is all offered within the Self;
for just as a seed that is healthy but deprived of a supporting medium does not sprout, [so too does the offering fail without the Self]. 6.40.
Likewise, a subtle seed of merit would be fruitless if it were without support;
just as a seed sown in fertile fields becomes a fruitful harvest. (6.41)
In the same way, even a small amount of merit becomes inexhaustible through taking refuge in Śiva;
therefore, whatever pleases one's own heart, one should offer that to the Lord.

One who desires the fruit [of their merit] should bestow each of those things upon the devotees of the Lord; likewise, whoever constructs a jeweled floor for Śiva or for the Guru [should do so]. (6.43)
Whoever prepares a beautiful offering for the purpose of a meal with leaves and flowers—[the merit] is calculated according to the number of those leaves and flowers. (6.44)
For that many thousands of years, he is honored in the world of the gods, especially if one offers leaves of the *palāśa*, the *kadalī* (plantain), and the *padma* (lotus). (6.45)
Listen to what fruit one obtains after giving [it] to Śiva, the Guru: for as many as are the number of its leaves offered to the Lord, [so many merits shall he gain]. (6.46)
For as many tens of thousands of years as he offers betel leaves and areca nuts, so long shall he enjoy pleasures in this world.
For as many hundreds of thousands of years as there are grains of pure conch powder that one might offer to the Guru, for so long is one honored in the world of Śiva.
Listen to the fruit of his merit for the sake of perfecting the preparation of betel: as many betel leaves as he may consume along with the measure of lime powder. (6.49)
For that many thousands of years, one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
[so too by offering] nutmeg with kaṅkola, as well as jasmine, musk, and blue lotus.
Thus, one should diligently offer these fragrant fruits;
for each fruit, through great enjoyments, one shall [attain] a hundred thousand years.
He sports in the city of Śiva by means of a desire-yielding celestial chariot,
[remaining] for a duration of only a moment in the presence of the Guru, who is Śiva, like a grain of camphor.
He who offers a vessel for betel nuts, betel leaves, and areca nuts is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for ten million years.
He who offers even a small vessel as a worthy recipient to anyone shall be honored in the world of Śiva with enjoyments for eighty million years. (6.54)
He who gives clods of earth, pieces of wood, or fragments of bamboo at a shrine of Śiva rejoices in the auspicious world for fourteen million years. (6.55)
A man shall obtain vast divine enjoyments in the city of Śiva—
ruby, water-pots, bowls, cooking vessels, and various sets of utensils.
Having given to them water-receptacles with lids made of clay, cloth, or wood, one is glorified in the world of Śiva. (6.57)
By giving vessels made of bamboo or gourd, one attains the city of Śiva;
likewise by giving water from a five-bristled broom, cow dung, collyrium, and a cloth.
One should offer a pedestal made of an earthen jar; such a person shall obtain enjoyments in the city of Śiva.
This applies to one who offers flowers, incense, perfumes, curd, milk, ghee, and water. (6.59)
He who gives supporting vessels made of bamboo, palm wood, or similar materials, as well as a flower-basket for holding offerings, goes to the world of Śiva. (6.60)
Whoever should give such things as these shall attain the world of Śiva;
likewise, whoever should present vessels such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles for the purpose of the *homa* sacrifice.
He who gives a mountain of salt combined with all the mineral elements is honored in the world of Śiva for ten million years by those of great fortune.
Or likewise for Śiva or for the Guru—listen to the fruit of his merit:
for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas.
That man, joined with the lineage-holding [state], shall dwell in the City of Śiva,
traveling in glorious celestial palaces provided with all objects of desire.
After enjoying vast pleasures, at the end of that time, that lord of the earth [obtained] realgar,
yellow orpiment, royal-lead ore, and vermilion.
Gairika, Maṇidanta, and likewise Hematoya as the eighth; and whoever [prepared] that best of mountains fashioned from śāli rice—6.66.
Listen to the fruit of his merit for [giving] to Śiva or to the Guru:
for more than a hundred crores of kalpas, he enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who [offers] a mountain of barley endowed with peaks of all kinds of grain, accompanied by rivers of ghee and oil. (6.68)
For more than a hundred billion eons, he enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva together with all those born of his lineage; at the end of that time, he becomes a lord of the earth.
The man who, having fashioned a sesame-cow upon a black antelope skin, should give it as a gift,
would obtain that same fruit which results from the gift of a tawny cow.
Having fashioned a cow made of ghee in a bronze vessel together with gold ornaments,
and having offered it, a man obtains the entire fruit of the gift of a cow.
Whoever, having placed a measure of salt (*lavaṇāḍhaka*) upon a leopard skin, should give it away, shall obtain that merit which comes from the gift of all flavors without exception. (6.72)
One should fashion a mountain named Mārīca with half a *marica*;
one should offer cumin first, and then the excellent *hiṅgu*, which belongs to Agni. (6.73)
One should place jaggery and ginger in the south, nāgakeśara in the southwest,
long pepper in the west, and black cumin in the northwest.
Ajamoda should be placed in the north, and cinnamon and cardamom in the northeast; kustumburu should be offered [there as well], situated outside the enclosure wall.
In the intervals between the quarters, one should place Saindhava salt all around;
with water containing flowers and unbroken rice grains, one should offer it for the sake of Śiva.
For as many islands as there are in total on that mountain,
for that many hundreds of years after [death], he enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva.
Having placed the kūśmāṇḍa in the center, one should set the kāliṅga in the east;
in the south, the milk-gourd (kṣīratumbī), and in the west, the eggplant (vṛntāka).
Having established *paṭīśānya* in the northeast, one should place *karkaṭī* under the deity Īśa;
and one should place *gaja* and *paṭola*, which are sweet, under the deity Agni.
One should place *kāravella* gourds in the southwest and nimba fruits in the northwest,
as well as various other kinds of fruits, outside [the pavilion].
Having worshipped the mountain of fruit on all sides with flowers and incense,
one should prostrate and offer it either to Śiva or to the Guru.
For as many thousands of years as there are fruits counted from the center of those islands, for that long one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having placed the radish in the center, the root of the *vāla* plant to its east;
having placed the *vāstuka* in the southeast, and the salty *vāstuka* in the south.
One should place Pālakyā in the southwest, install Sumukha in the west,
Kuhadraka in the northwest, and Tālikī in the north.
Having placed the kusumbha vegetable in the northeast and all other vegetables outside of that,
one should offer them to Śiva according to the previously established sequence.
For as many thousands of years as there are leaves on its roots and stalks, he is honored in the world of Rudra.
Having given two *pala* of *guggulu* resin from the mountain, one obtains great enjoyments; by giving it mixed with molasses, one dwells in heaven for twice ten million years. (6.87)
By devotedly offering molasses, ginger, salt, and mango blossoms to the Guru, one shall obtain supreme good fortune. (6.88)
Or, having made the earth endowed with great jewels and offered it to Śarva by means of a formal hand-consecration, one is born equal to Śiva.
Diamond, sapphire, lapis lazuli, ruby, pearl, emerald, and gold—these indeed are the seven great jewels. (6.90)
And as for the king who would give a lion-throne endowed with great jewels and various minor gems— listen to the fruit of his merit.
Accompanied by his thirty kinsmen, together with his harem and retinue,
and joined by all his servants, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there, possessing prowess equal to Śiva, he shall remain until the time of the great dissolution; at its conclusion, he shall attain liberation.
If he should desire sovereignty, then, being fully concentrated,
he would become the lord of the earth consisting of seven continents and oceans.
Having ruled kingdoms for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of births, he shall at the end once again go to the city of Śiva.
This very same fruit should be known to result from [offering] crowns, ornaments, and so forth;
by the gift of a jeweled throne, one should present sandals. (6.96)
He who would give even a single pure grain of wheat as an offering to Śiva shall dwell happily in the auspicious world until the dissolution of all things.
By the gift of sapphire and by the gift of lapis lazuli,
one rejoices in manifold enjoyments for ten million eons in the city of Śiva.
He who offers even a ruby the size of a lentil, provided it is of excellent quality,
rejoices for eternal time after presenting it to Śarva.
Having offered a single part of pure pearl,
one rejoices for ten million kalpas in the divine realm of Śiva, enjoying celestial pleasures.
Having offered a pure, large-winged insect the size of a barley grain to Śiva,
one rejoices today in the world of Śiva for imperishable time.
And he who, having fashioned even a flower the size of a single *māṣaka* from gold, offers it to Śarva, shall dwell in heaven for ten million years. (6.102)
The man who gives small jewels set in gold to Śambhu rejoices in the world of Śiva for ten million times ten thousand kalpas.
Just as a great jewel is beautiful, so too, it should be understood that the greater the merit resulting from the gift of Śiva, the more magnificent it is. (6.104)
On that extensive area of ground, one should fashion Jambudvīpa,
complete with its eight enclosures and adorned by the eight lords of mountains. (6.105)
In the middle of that, one should cause to be built the divine and supreme temple of Meru,
filled with many peaks and inhabited by all the immortals.
On the outside, it was covered with gold, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
provided with four neck-ornaments, and marked with the signs of the eyes.
It was endowed with groves in the four directions, joined by four arrows,
and provided with a rampart surrounding the four cities.
Whoever should cause to be built a palace like Mount Meru, adorned with gold and jewels and surrounded by groves, shall obtain infinite fruit.
Just as the number of atoms of earth and water cannot be known, so too the merit of a shrine of Śiva cannot be numbered. (6.110)
Accompanied by his thirty clansmen, attended by all his servants,
and joined by his wife, sons, friends, and all his kinsmen.
Accompanied by all his attendants and subordinates, together with his entire host without exception,
he is worshipped throughout the whole world just as Śiva himself is.
Nor would he return again to the wretched human world;
omniscient and perfected, he remains liberated within his own self.
He who, having joyfully established a forest for Śiva that rises from the waters of the ocean,
should always hold in his hand that which is adorned by the Daṇḍaka forest.
In various places, they adorned the Bhūtanātha temple or the moon-chamber; or else, lofty rows of pillars rose up toward the altar.
Or else, one should have an image of the Lord made of gold, endowed with all the auspicious marks, serene in appearance, and one man’s height tall.
She holds a trident in her right hand and bestows boons and fearlessness;
in her [other] right hand she holds a rosary, and she is adorned with matted hair and flowers.
Seated upon a lotus throne or standing upon a bull, elevated high;
or situated within a celestial chariot, or mounted on a chariot, or standing upon an altar, she is endowed with radiant splendor.
With a gentle face or a terrifying one, possessing a form as formidable as Mahābhairava,
she stands exceedingly tall and very broad, poised in dance and established in yoga.
In the absence of gold, one should make it of pure silver; or else, it may be made of brass, or even of copper, clay, stone, or wood.
One should paint [the deity] on a cloth, a wall, or even a wooden panel, using all the colors in their proper forms, with devotion and according to one's means. (6.121)
One should indeed, without any hesitation, represent Pārvatī either alone with her retinue, or accompanied by the Gaṇas and attended by the door-keeper. (6.122)
Or one should have a pedestal made of silver, copper, or brass;
it may have four faces or a single face, with its exterior refined with gold. (6.123)
Having caused many distinct faces to be fashioned for Śiva, who possesses manifold forms— faces both gentle and terrifying— (6.124)
During the chariot procession of Śiva, one should show the people those [images] adorned with various ornaments and fashioned from gold and silver.
Whatever merits have been described individually and in brief,
by performing them all as one for me, one shall obtain their inexhaustible fruit.
Together with his mother and father, by means of ten families on each side,
he was joined by his wife, sons, friends, and so forth, as well as by servants and kinsmen. (6.127)
Possessing ten thousand celestial palaces endowed with all desirable things,
he himself enjoys great luxuries and, in the end, shall attain liberation.
One should drive in stakes adorned with mirrors at the edge of the pillars of the pavilion,
where people, having performed their ablutions, offer worship with *bilva* leaves.
Having assumed the form of Kālakāla, whoever should perform the ritual of staking within the hermitage of Śiva and worship [it] day after day for the benefit of all the worlds; 6.130.

O King, he who would establish in a Śiva-hermitage a water-clock (ghaṭī) that either flows out or fills up during a full watch (sadāyāma), for the purpose of measuring the duration of the incense-offering time, [attains great merit]. 6.131.
Having performed even one of these meritorious deeds and being freed from evil,
a man shall reach the world of Śiva and become omniscient and happy.
I shall describe the chariot procession of Śiva, the Supreme Self, which was fashioned by a master craftsman for the benefit of all the worlds. (6.133)
Having placed [the deity] in the center of the chariot, one should fix it like a sacrificial post;
the most beautiful celestial mansion (vimāna) is to be fashioned as situated in the middle of that post.
It should be five stories high or three stories high, constructed with sturdy bamboo, well-fastened by mechanical means, and securely bound with ropes. (6.135)
It should be provided with five types of grain-offerings, endowed with various modes of devotion,
and covered with multicolored cloths or fabrics adorned with pigments.
Adorned with hanging tassels, cords, and ribbons, and decorated with bells and chowries,
it was brilliantly illuminated by bubbles, crescent moons, and mirrors.
It was adorned with banana-tree half-flags, possessed great parasols and great banners,
was encircled by flower garlands, and endowed with every kind of beauty.
One should place the image of Īśvara, together with his retinue, within this great chariot-palace, in the first pavilion of the city made of gold.
And one should bind three openings and likewise make them external;
situated outside each city in all directions, they are supported within the small houses.
Having established the four faces of Śiva, one should worship them; for three days, one should perform bathing, ritual worship, and feeding.
On the full-moon festival of the month of Pauṣa, with the performance of dances and games, by those reciting auspicious songs, and with the resounding blasts of great musical instruments— (6.142)
On the fourth day, one should cause that chariot to be paraded along the royal highway;
then, having brought it back to its own place, one should also increase the remainder of those [offerings]. (6.143)
Having focused his mind, he should bring down the image of the Mother of the World;
this journey in a great celestial chariot may also be performed upon a cloth painting.
One should construct a mat capable of bearing a load using fresh and well-ripened bamboo;
it should be circular, twice as long [as it is wide], or square at the bottom with even sides. (6.145)
Bound everywhere with leather and supported by a great staff,
one should make the opening firmly secured with a bamboo ring.
Having placed those garments upon this mat, tie them securely with effort;
arrange all of them one above the other, and place the image in their midst. (6.147)
One should worship with pigments such as saffron and with variegated flowers, and with various offerings of ornaments, including long-hanging pearl necklaces. (6.148)
Having placed two firm bands across the middle of the large chariot, arranged one above the other and provided with a hole in the center. (6.149)
Having placed the lower portion of the central shaft upon auspicious, perforated supports,
one should fasten it with effort and fix eight banners at the midpoint of the shaft.
One should have the back of the mat covered everywhere with cloth;
and upon that cloth, one should depict Soma together with his retinue, and Śiva together with his bull.
One should adorn the platform on all sides with garlands and strings of various flowers,
and with tassels, networks of small bells, and ornaments of bells and yak-tail whisks.
Accompanied by great and special offerings and filled with curiosity, one should arrange the beauty of the path with the performance of musical instruments and ritual services. (6.153)
One should carefully cause that chariot to be driven all around by way of the royal highway;
then, having brought it back to one's own hermitage, one should station it nearby.
Then one should make a great sound accompanied by three claps of the hands;
when the world has thus become silent, one should maintain that state of peace here.
May there be welfare for the entire world, welfare for cows and brahmins, and may there be welfare for kings, for their devotees, and for all people. (6.156)
May the king attain victory and may he prosper with his sons and grandsons; may he be devoted to righteousness and intent upon the welfare of his subjects. (6.157)
May the rain-cloud pour forth in due season, may there be an abundance of crops, and through plenty may security be attained; may success in all undertakings arise. (6.158)
May your faults go to destruction and may your virtues attain stability;
may your cows, abounding in much milk, be joyful and well-nourished.
Having thus recited the Great Peace of Śiva for the world in due order,
and having increased it, he then [recites] the remainder, which is the Sovereign Power that fulfills all desires.
Taking up a garland of *śiva* flowers and accompanied by female attendants,
he should carry a vessel filled with fruits and edible offerings and present it.
And that son of a god should carry the bowl upon his head, wearing a turban;
adorned, dressed in white, righteous, and always pure. (6.162)
Then, having lifted it up, the wise man should hold it with his hand;
another person here, a partaker of the Śiva-dharma, should proclaim [the mantra]. (6.163)
Just as water contained in a jar flows out incessantly, so too does the life-span of all people flow away day and night. (6.164)
Since one must inevitably depart, having abandoned everything against one's will, why is this wealth not given for the sake of provisions for the journey? (6.165)
Wife, sons, friends, father, mother, and kinsmen—none of these, nor even wealth, remain for the sake of the deceased in the world beyond. (6.166)
There is no friend equal to the Dharma, there is no companion equal to the Dharma; for the Dharma follows the man who has been abandoned by all others. (6.167)
Therefore, he who, for the sake of the Dharma, increases his remaining wealth,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Śiva.
To him who increases his remaining wealth further and further, this most excellent [daughter] should be given, for by him no other [debt] shall increase. (6.169)
Thus, one should increase the middle [portion], or the remaining [portion] should be made smaller;
then these [offerings] should be presented to them for the pacification of all sorrow. (6.170)
By whomsoever this most excellent, vast [garland], remaining from Śiva, has been taken, it should be brought to his home in the very same manner, borne upon the head. (6.171)

Then, having reached the door of the house with banners, parasols, celestial chariots, and the like, accompanied by the sounds of great musical instruments, one should worship it and cause [the image] to enter.
One should give to one's kinsmen, wives, servants, and relatives;
and one should devoutly satisfy with offerings those who carry musical instruments and banners while they are bowed down. (6.173)
Listen now to the fruit of the dharma for one who is thus taken with devotion to the excellent house of Śiva along the royal road with splendor. (6.174)
Freed from all sins and accompanied by his entire family,
he attains the world of Śiva along with his servants and attendants.
There, with divine and great enjoyments and celestial palaces that fulfill all desires, he sports for ten million eons; at the end, he shall attain nirvāṇa.
Listen attentively to the fruit obtained by one who, with such adornment, organizes a procession for the chariot and provides various kinds of food and edibles. (6.177)
Freed from all sins without exception, accompanied by all his servants, having uplifted thirty generations of his lineage, together with his friends and kinsmen, he [attains liberation]. (6.178)
Surrounded by magnificent celestial women, he dwells in glorious great celestial palaces (mahāvimāna) endowed with all desirable things, divine, and providing the abode for movement at will.
By his own will, he sports with enjoyments for ten million eons in the city of Śiva;
then, having attained the yoga of knowledge, he is liberated from saṃsāra.
Listen to the fruit obtained by one who, intent on fasting and patient, walks either in front of or behind Śiva during his chariot procession. (6.181)
Freed from all sins without exception, pure, and having gone to the city of Śiva,
he rejoices for eighty eons in vehicles comparable to great chariots.
There were thousands of decorations consisting of banners, parasols, and flags; lamps, mirrors, and yak-tail whisks; incense, canopies, and water-jars. (6.183)
Having taken [them], they go before [the deity] either by their own will or by the will of another; through contact, curiosity, or gain, they proceed to the world of Śiva. (6.184)
Those who behold the chariot procession of Śiva with devotion—whether by chance or out of curiosity—they too go to the city of Śiva. (6.185)
During the chariot procession, one should perform various spectacles, including those ending with the *nānāyatna* and *diśeṣa*, and the adorned [Queen] shall take her delight.
Those men, having approached Śiva as lords of the Gaṇas, sport with various divine enjoyments in the abode of Rudra for twenty kalpas.
By means of that great assembly of knowledge and by means of the auspicious chariot, individual souls who have died go to the world of Śiva; of this there is no doubt.
At Śrīparvata, Mahākāla, Vārāṇasī, and Mahālaya;
at Jalpeśvara, Kurukṣetra, Kedāra, and Maṇḍaleśvara.
At Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Sthaleśvara;
at Bhīmeśvara, Suvarṇākṣa, and likewise in the Kālañjara forest.
And all living beings, both moving and stationary, who die in these and other such sacred fields of Śiva, go to the world of Śiva.
Prayāga is the tīrtha that fulfills desires, while Avimukta is the one for those committed to the ultimate goal;
Śrīparvata should also be known as bestowing success both in this world and the next. (6.192)
Even one who, while traveling elsewhere, should happen to see the highly meritorious Śrīparvata even by chance, shall go to the city of Śiva.
He who visits the sacred sites of Śiva is liberated from all sins;
even one burdened by sin, having attained the knowledge of Śiva, shall reach nirvāṇa.
He who, at sacred sites, diligently performs a śrāddha on Śivarātri in accordance with the time and the equinox (viṣuva), [attains the highest goal].
He was traveling on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, appearing tranquil yet bewildered, crying out "Alas! Alas!", and unconscious;
afflicted by hunger and thirst in this world, his feet were covered in dust as he moved with haste.
Having diligently refreshed him with water as if restoring a withered splendor, what man could be his equal by the offering of water for the feet and a seat? (6.197)
For as many morsels of that food as those whose sins have been washed away by the sacred ford consume,
for that many thousands of years do those givers dwell in the city of Śiva.
The man who gives a well-lactating buffalo for the sake of a Śiva-sacrifice rejoices in the world of Śiva for a hundred times ten million yugas.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who gives a single, well-nourished, and prolific she-goat to a distressed devotee of Śiva. (6.200)
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on that [cow], he is honored in the world of Rudra within the families born from her.
By offering a dark-complexioned girl with soft body hair to his teacher, a man obtains the fruit of having given gold equal in weight to every single hair on her body. (6.202)
Accompanied by his followers, he sports with all-enjoyable pleasures in celestial palaces filled with elephants, horses, and chariots, within the city of Śiva for ten million eons.
Having offered a well-nourished, unblemished mule to his teacher,
a man enjoys companionship along with all necessary requisites and various pleasures in the city of Śiva.
For ten million times ten million eons, he shall dwell in glorious celestial palaces yoked with divine horses that fulfill all desires; at the end of that time, he shall become a lord of the earth.
Even if one should prepare a palanquin for a teacher who is peaceful and self-controlled for a distance of only a single yojana, hear now the fruit of that merit. (6.206)
With a thousand celestial palaces endowed with all desirable things,
he enjoys pleasures for more than ten million times ten thousand eons in the city of Śiva.
A goat, a ram, a peacock, a cock, a myna bird, a parrot—these and other such toys for children, and so forth. (6.208)
Having offered [this] to Skanda, one shall attain union with him;
after enjoying vast pleasures, at the end of that, one shall become the best of the twice-born.
One should give pestles, mortars, and other household utensils to those residing in the temple of Śiva; hear now the fruit of that merit. (6.210)
For each kalpa, a person shall dwell for one kalpa in heaven with enjoyments consisting of household furnishings; at the end of that, he shall become a householder once more.
Having given a well-fashioned circular seat for a crore [of people] made of dates, palm leaves, or leather, one shall attain the world of Śiva. (6.212)
In the winter, at the time of the morning mist, by kindling a fire for the sake of warming himself, one is glorified in the world of Śiva among the yogins of Śiva. (6.213)
Having enjoyed pleasures for a hundred billion eons in celestial palaces that fulfill all desires and blaze with the radiance of ten thousand suns, that lord of the earth—
He who feeds, according to his ability, a Śiva-yogin traveling through a wilderness or a foreign land, is glorified in the world of Śiva. (6.215)
Whoever holds an umbrella for a Śiva-yogin walking in the summer shall,
upon death, obtain the entire earth under a single umbrella.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who has set out upon the yoga of Śiva, who provides a path, a mat, and necessary implements. (6.217)
Having enjoyed pleasures for more than ten thousand aeons in the city of Śiva,
at the end of that time, he shall attain a kingdom endowed with all sovereign powers.
By performing oil massage, dry rubbing, and bathing for an afflicted Śiva-yogin, a person attains great enjoyments in the city of Śiva for many kalpas. (6.219)
By respectfully removing the food-leavings of Śiva-yogins, a person obtains the fruit of the gift of ten cows. (6.220)
The food remains of the Śiva-yogins should be known as equal to the five products of the cow;
by eating that, one attains purification even from a great sin. (6.221)
And a woman, having eaten [of this], shall obtain a virtuous son who is the support of his lineage, endowed with good qualities, fit for sovereignty, wealthy, and devoted to righteousness. (6.222)
And whatever a householder devoted to Śiva might provide for the sake of a Śiva-sacrifice, he shall obtain the supreme fruit of that great act. (6.223)
Whoever diligently observes this vow for Śiva and Umā with devotion for one year shall obtain the complete fruit of giving away a hundred thousand cows.
In the morning, one should offer a well-prepared ball of food mixed with ghee and *dūrvā* grass to young calves;
hear now the meritorious fruit of that act. (6.225)
For as long as one provides drink and food for those with young calves,
for that long does one enjoy eighty thousand pleasures in the city of Śiva.
He who provides a livelihood for widows, the protectorless,
and the elderly is honored in the world of Śiva until the final dissolution of all beings.
Whoever should diligently provide food for all living beings would obtain that same fruit as one who gives away the entire earth filled with jewels. (6.228)
Whatever vows and gifts for discipline are established in the world, one should perform them according to that very same procedure with the Śiva-mantra. (6.229)
By offering [this] to Rudra, to Rudrāṇī, and to the Six-faced One,
a man shall obtain vast and divine enjoyments in the city of Śiva.
Furthermore, whoever should give a pair of scissors for the removal of the afflictions of hair shall be liberated from all afflictions and become happy in the world of Śiva. (6.231)
One should give a nose-cleanser and forceps to a practitioner of Śiva-yoga;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for ten million years. (6.232)
Having given a nail-cutter, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
for a hundred thousand years, one is glorified in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments. // 6.233 //
Having given a collyrium probe made of iron or other materials to a Śiva-yogin, one shall attain enjoyments in the city of Śiva and obtain the eye of knowledge. (6.234)
Having given an ear-cleaner made of iron or other materials to a Śiva-yogin,
one is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for ten million years.
He who gives a needle for cleaning a loincloth to a devotee of Śiva is honored in the world of Śiva for one hundred and fifty thousand years.
Having offered a needle together with thread to the Śiva-yogins,
he sports for a hundred thousand years with great enjoyments in the city of Śiva.
He who gives a well-crafted leaf-piercing needle to Śiva-yogins is honored in the world of Śiva with great enjoyments for a hundred thousand years. (6.238)
He who gives books and other such items that accomplish all purposes and goals rejoices with great enjoyments in the city of Śiva for five hundred thousand [aeons]. (6.239)
Whoever gives śamī wood, grass, and other such materials, as well as provides for their cutting,
shall sport in the world of Śiva for four hundred thousand years.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who gives a large metal implement, such as an axe and so forth, for the use of Śiva’s hermitage. (6.241)
For as many hundreds of thousands of years as there are counts of those iron implements, for that long one is honored in the world of Śiva.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who provides bows, swords, weapons, and the like for the protection of the wealth of Śiva’s shrines. (6.243)
Furthermore, for each individual weapon that is fully understood,
one is honored in the world of Śiva with enjoyments for eighty million years.
Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who offers flowers to Śiva or to the Guru for the sake of his own enjoyment or for the sake of his servants. (6.245)
As many as there are mutual connections among its parts,
for that many hundred thousand years he rejoices in the world of Śiva.
Having searched for what was lost or stolen, one should report the recovered wealth to Śiva alone as being of the nature of Śiva; hear now the fruit of his merit. (6.247)
It is traditionally taught that the fruit of giving that wealth to Śiva beforehand is such that, having recovered what was lost and giving it again, one obtains a hundredfold merit. (6.248)
If property belonging to the gods that has been stolen or lost is sought with effort but cannot be recovered, then he shall receive a reward double [the value of] that property. (6.249)
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who offers a copper pitcher, a cauldron, or similar vessels to Śiva, who is himself of the nature of Śiva and to Śiva alone. (6.250)
It is traditionally taught that whatever wealth one first offers for the sake of Śiva is considered to bear fruit;
having brought back what was lost, one obtains a hundredfold merit once again.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who uses it for bathing and as a support; the calculation of that fruit remains established in the copper vessel. (6.252)
He who gives a vessel as a support for leaves, flowers, or other offerings rejoices in the city of Śiva for many millions of years.
Whatever merit belongs to the giver of that object, all of that merit shall belong to him who gives even some small article as a requisite to those in need of wealth. (6.254)
Whatever object one provides, by that one shall obtain the fruit of its gift; so too for one who provides clean, dyed garments for the Śiva-yogins with alkaline substances and the like. (6.255)
He who gives a woolen blanket (*kambala*) filled with cloth and joined with a floral border shall be freed from the impurity of sin and attain the world of Śiva. (6.256)
One should give [this] to the Śiva-yogins; hear now the fruit of that merit: for as many threads as there are in those garments, for that many [years]... (6.257)
He who gives smooth, white garments to a Śiva-yogin enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva for as many thousands of years as there are threads in those garments. (6.258)
Listen to the fruit of his merit for offering variegated garments out of devotion to him:
it lasts as long as the number of threads in those fine garments is calculated. (6.259)
For that many yugas he is honored in the world of Śiva with enjoyments;
[he who offers] a broad conch-vessel or even a very beautiful container.
One should give [these] to the yogis of Śiva; hear now the fruit of that merit:
mounted upon a divine celestial chariot endowed with all objects of desire, (he shall attain liberation). 6.261
He is honored in the world of Śiva for more than ten million times ten thousand aeons;
likewise, beautiful and stainless vessels such as mother-of-pearl and the like [yield great merit]. (6.262)
By offering [food] to Śiva-yogins with a conch-shell vessel, one obtains half the fruit;
it is taught that the fruit of crystal vessels is equal to that of the conch.
For vessels made of stone, half of that [measure] is prescribed;
for vessels made of bell-metal, conch, or bamboo, half of that again is prescribed when they are offered.
The merit of others such as these is equal to half a tree;
the merit in the offering of fruit and vessels is equal to half a bamboo shoot. (6.265)
And [the gift] of various leaf-cups or the heartwood of trees, or half a fruit;
or those who give copper and bronze vessels that are polished and stainless—6.266.
Whoever should give a vessel of copper, bell-metal, or the three metals (triloha) with three legs to a Śiva-yogin for the purpose of bathing, eating, and drinking; (6.267)

Regarding food and the vessel for food, hear now the fruit of that [offering] to the Guru; as many palas as there are in the measure of that food, so many [years] shall he dwell in the three worlds. (6.268)
Having given a three-legged vessel made of iron and having honored it for a Śiva-yogin, one enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva for as many thousands of yugas as there are legs. (6.269)
A man who gives a shelter for a mendicant’s bowl, even as small as a begging bowl, shall dwell in the city of Śiva for ten kalpas with great enjoyments. (6.270)
Whether it be made of bamboo or even of wood, hear now the fruit of its merit:
established upon a great celestial chariot, he shall be endowed with the enjoyment of divine women.
For a thousand cycles of the four yugas, he enjoys pleasures in the city of Śiva, [possessing] an alms-bowl for a face-cover and garments fashioned from leaves and other materials. (6.272)
Having given [these], a man shall dwell for one kalpa in the city of Śiva; this applies also to one who provides shelter, or [gives] an alms-bowl or a water-pot.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who prepares [an image] with cloth, thread, and so forth: it is equal to the number of threads that are spun from that purified cloth. (6.274)
For that many thousands of years, he is honored in the world of Rudra;
[he who uses] a rope, bark, or hair for his seat, or relies upon a sling and vessels. 6.275.
He who, having prepared a garland, a yoke-cord, a rein, or even a rope, and likewise other such objects, should offer them; 6.276.

Listen to the fruit of his merit for the purpose of providing fodder for Śiva’s cattle: as many times as there are strands of that rope, so many [years] shall he give [merit] to the herd of Śiva’s cows. (6.277)
For that long, the embodied soul is honored in the world of Śiva;
indeed, in proportion as the garment is dear and beautiful, so too [is his reward]. (6.278)
In that same way, the great merit from such giving increases further and further for one who, when asked, points out the path or [returns] lost cattle and so forth. (6.279)
He obtains merit equal to the gift of a cow, as well as wisdom and happiness;
by providing aid to the afflicted, he goes to heaven—of this there is no doubt.
Having extracted even a thorn, how much more so one of great virtue?
He who should point out the giver of food, drink, and medicine— (6.281)
The fruit corresponding to that [gift] should be understood to belong to the giver for those who are afflicted;
his obstructed karma remains for the sake of Śiva, provided it is not [otherwise] exhausted.
