By giving even a small portion of a sacrificial accessory, one obtains the fruit of the sacrifice—even if it be merely a blade of kāśa or kuśa grass, a thread, cow dung, or fuel for the sacred fire. (6.283)

I shall explain in brief that which should be given with devotion by all devotees of Śiva for the purpose of utilizing it in the Śiva-sacrifice (śivayajña). Having given [this], one should know that the fruit of the sacrifice is obtained; how much more so, then, from the gift of material objects? (6.284)
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Śivopaniṣad, concerning the bestowal of fruits and auxiliary means.
Now, for the sake of heaven and liberation, I shall briefly proclaim the unsurpassed conduct of Śiva (śivācāra) for all devotees of Śiva. 7.1
Since Śiva bestows gifts for the welfare of all beings, he remains present in the form of the Guru;
therefore, one should constantly worship the Guru.
Just as one would not imagine the presence of Śiva in a linga that lacks the proper characteristics,
likewise one should not imagine his presence in a guru who possesses little scriptural knowledge.
Only one who knows the reality of the purpose of Śiva-knowledge, having established himself as Śiva within the serene-minded Guru, imparts knowledge; no other indeed does so. (7.4)
And one should worship the guru with devotion as if he were Śiva, by means of salutation,
with palms joined in reverence at the three junctions of the day, having placed the head upon the ground.

A wise person should not pay homage to a teacher who is not secluded, who has not rinsed his mouth, who is walking about restlessly, who is distracted, or who is moving along while absorbed in meditative concentration.
During the exposition, at its conclusion, upon being questioned, after bathing or eating, and after eating while lying down to sleep, one should always pay homage to the guru. (7.7)
One desiring to go to another village should circumambulate the teacher from left to right;
and upon returning, one should again perform a prostration with all limbs. (7.8)
On all festival days, one should offer fragrant purifiers; likewise at the commencement of the knowledge of Śiva, and upon departing for or returning from a journey. (7.9)
One should perform this at the commencement of the vows of the Śiva-dharma and at their conclusion;
likewise, for the sake of propitiating one who is angry, and similarly after conquering an enemy.

On an auspicious day, during the pacification of the planets, at initiation, upon attaining the status of a teacher accompanied by a sacrificial fee, and during the rite of purification and the installation of the image.
One should not wear shoes, an umbrella, a bed, clothing, a seat, ornaments, an alms-bowl, a staff, or a rosary that belong to one's teacher. (7.12)
One should not engage in laughing, spitting, slapping one's arms, loud speaking, yawning, stretching out the legs, or walking in the presence of a teacher. (7.13)
He should have inferior food, drink, and clothing, and his bed and seat should be lower than those of the teacher; he should not remain as he pleases, and he should avoid quarreling. (7.14)
One should not stand upwind or downwind of one's teacher; nor should one ever stand in a place where there is no shelter, nor should one speak anything disparagingly of the teacher.
One should not converse with one's teacher while distracted by something else, nor while eating, nor while standing with one's back turned, nor while lying down, nor while seated. (7.16)
Upon seeing his teacher approaching, he should rise quickly from afar;
and when permitted by the teacher, he should sit down behind him.
One should not cover the neck, nor should one hang anything there;
nor should one wash one's feet or bathe where the teacher is standing and might see it.

One should not perform the cleaning of teeth, anointing with oil, bathing, massaging, or the act of applying fragrant unguents, nor the voiding of excrement or the changing of clothes, while the teacher is looking on. (7.19)
Whatever the guru may offer that is near to the house, the disciple, keeping his face turned toward [the guru], should receive it in his joined palms or in a vessel before him.
Whatever the teacher may offer, one should stand before him with a bowed head and receive it with both hands, placing it securely. (7.21)
One should not utter the name of the guru alone, even when he is out of sight; nor should one address another who holds an equal rank by that same name. (7.22)
If one's own guru and his guru should ever be equal [in status], then the guru of those two is to be honored, and one's own guru [is to be honored] by his command. (7.23)
One should not eat without having offered [food] to him, and after eating, one should offer it to him.
One should not go outside on any business without having informed the teacher. (7.24)
Having performed the ritual action by the teacher's command, he should report its completion;
and having performed all his daily duties, he should study by the teacher's command. (7.25)
Earth, ashes, cow dung, water, leaves, flowers, fuel, and sacrificial wood—these eight items are sufficient; one should collect them for the sake of the teacher. (7.26)
One should bring medicine, food, vessels, clothing, bedding, and seats for the guru with every effort, having entreated the lords of wealth.
One should not violate the command of the guru, even at the cost of one's life;
by carrying out his command, one attains liberation, but by transgressing it, one goes to hell. (7.28)
One should wander the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves;
for the sake of accomplishing the medicine of the guru, one may even go to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Whatever the guru may command, one should do it without hesitation;
for gurus are never to be questioned in any matter whatsoever. (7.30)
One should not cause [the teacher] who is sitting comfortably to rise, nor should one wake him from sleep;
one should approach the seated teacher while remaining seated, or go toward him when he is standing.

One should carefully cause the teacher to rest while he is traveling on the road; and knowing him to be afflicted by hunger or thirst, or having bathed, one should feed him when he is capable of eating. (7.32)
One should diligently perform oil massage, dry rubbing, bathing, eating, spitting, wiping, massaging the limbs, and the anointing of the feet at night. (7.33)
In the morning, having provided the means for adornment, the sweeping and the application of collyrium should be performed,
along with the scattering of various flowers in the magnificent assembly hall for exposition.
Having prepared the venerable seat for the guru and the book of the knowledge of Śiva, he should remain there, awaiting the guru’s arrival in due order. (7.35)
Upon hearing censure or slander of the guru, one should cover one's ears; otherwise, one should slither away or restrain [the speaker] through skillful means. (7.36)

One should not do anything displeasing to the guru, whether one is being oppressed by him or even rescued by him; nor should one utter his words [in a disrespectful manner], for by so doing, one would go to hell. (7.37)
The guru alone is the father, the guru alone is the mother; the guru alone is the supreme Śiva.
For one whose conviction in this is certain, liberation is not far off.
Whatever the master or lord may do regarding food, conduct, and religious duties, one should follow that very same way without questioning the reason. (7.39)
Sacrifices, austerities, and various observances—all these are undoubtedly accomplished through the word of the guru. (7.40)
Who would not honor him who lifts up with his own hand of the knowledge of Śiva the person submerged in the mire of ignorance? (7.41)
Thus, whoever constantly worships the Lord residing within the form of the Guru, being liberated from all sins, attains the supreme state. (7.42)
Having bathed with water or with ashes, and wearing white garments and the sacred thread,
the Guru should place a flower containing a blade of dūrvā grass upon the head [of the disciple].
One should apply yellow pigment (rocanā) to oneself, burn incense upon one's body, and wear a ring, a rosary, and an earring. (7.44)
Such a glorious guru should always remain composed, for the guru dwells as Sadāśiva for the sake of imparting knowledge. (7.45)
He should always wear sandals made of soft leather,
and having taken up a staff or an umbrella, he may wander outside the hermitage.
The Guru should not place his foot on the ground without an interposition;
having stepped upon a footstool of *kuśa* grass, he should prepare it for the purpose of libation.
Having prepared foot-rests with leaves and other materials, he should enter the temple; and having placed his feet upon a footstool,
he should always eat while maintaining silence.
One should not wash one's feet in a vessel made of bronze or iron;
rather, one should perform the purification over a bed of grass and likewise sip water for rinsing on a second [bed of grass].
He should not wear dyed or gaudy clothing, nor flowers; he should not wear perfumes or garlands outside [the monastery], nor soiled garments. (7.50)
One should not step upon hair, bones, potsherds, cotton seeds, husks, impure substances, charcoal, ashes, or dust. (7.51)
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with one's nails; nor should one pluck leaves, flowers, fruits, bamboo, auspicious wood, or pieces of timber.
One should not rub such things or others with one's hands; one should not practice tooth-cleaning, nor should one pluck out body hair. (7.53)
One should not scratch the ground with one's feet, nor with clods of earth, wood, or the hand;
one should not pierce one's nails with the nails, nor should one scratch one's body with the nails.
A wise man should not repeatedly touch his head or beard with his fingernails, nor should he scratch himself or another person. (7.55)
One should scratch the body using prongs, teeth, or sticks made of gold, silver, or copper; or with bamboo, wood, *kāṣṭhīka*, or *vīraṇa* grass. (7.56)
One should not engage in idle chatter while looking about in various directions;
nor should one remain afflicted by grief, resting the cheek upon the hand.
One should not engage in restlessness with the hands, feet, speech, eyes, ears, genitals, anus, or stomach; thus one shall attain all goals. (7.58)
One should not harbor enmity toward anyone while life remains uncertain;
one should avoid sinful curiosity regarding worldly affairs and the twilight hours.
One should not enter houses, cities, or villages through side-gates;
by day one should not walk about with the head covered, and at night one should walk about having covered it.
One should not be prone to excessive wandering, nor should one enter from house to house;
one should not study what is not knowledge, but should practice the knowledge of Śiva.

One should not abandon that supreme Brahman which is the knowledge of Śiva once it has been undertaken; he who departs while still unaccomplished in Brahman is proclaimed a slayer of Brahman (brahmahā).
The disciple should stand with palms joined, wearing light clothing and facing north;
then the teacher, facing east, should recite the Śiva-mantra and teach him.
The excellent seat of the Guru should be quadrangular and very beautiful, fashioned from ivory and the like, or even inlaid with gold and jewels. (7.64)
If he has no desire to serve, no interest in the goal, and no dharma is observed; if there is neither devotion nor fame, but only cruelty—the teacher should not instruct him. (7.65)
In the presence of gods, fire, gurus, or assemblies for exposition, study, or debate;
when questioned or engaged in disputation; when speaking untruthfully; and during impurity—one should raise the right arm. (7.66)
One should remain perpetually humble under their authority, withdrawing one's limbs like a tortoise;
and when departing in their presence, one should do so preceded by a salutation.
One should not pass between a deity, fire, a guru, or a brahmin; nor should one offer or receive any object while standing between them. 7.68
One should not blow on the fire with one's mouth, nor place it beneath oneself, nor step over it; one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet at it. 7.69.
One should not kindle a fire in a place thick with grass, wood, and the like, or crowded with living beings; nor, once it is burning, should one cast anything into it.
Having brought fire at once, a wise person should maintain it with care; he should not himself extinguish a burning lamp.
Upon seeing one who observes the vow of Śiva, one should always rise up quickly;
then, resolving "This is Śiva," one should bow down with joy. (7.72)
When worshipped in the *liṅga*, Śiva bestows abundant enjoyments;
in the fire, he grants various supernatural powers (*siddhi*); and in the guru, he bestows liberation. (7.73)
Therefore, for the sake of liberation, one should worship the Lord residing within the form of the Guru;
through devotion to the Guru, one obtains knowledge, and from knowledge, one attains liberation. (7.74)
On all festival days, one should diligently worship Śiva;
one should create beauty within the temple and throughout all the places where the Guru resides.
Having installed a liṅga made of jewels upon a pedestal two *naris* high and endowed with every beauty, one should perform that which brings welfare to the world in that place. (7.76)
One should prepare an offering of food with various kinds of delicacies, and here one should feed those observing the vow, especially one's own guru. (7.77)
One should worship the knowledge of Śiva and cause it to be recited on the sacred festival days;
one should show it to the devotees of Śiva, having prepared a proper worship for it.
One should always speak kindly to them and also give them gifts according to one's ability;
when this is done, Maheśvara is especially pleased.
One should not utter words such as "cut," "broken," "dead," "lost," or "only non-existence"; rather, one should speak auspiciously. (7.80)
One should call a non-cow "cow," and an inauspicious thing "auspicious"; one should call a skull a "cranium" and speak of the supreme as "most auspicious. (7.81)
One should speak of Indra’s bow as a jeweled bow, burning wood and the like as sandalwood, one who has gone to heaven as deceased, and a yogin as having become Śiva. (7.82)
One should speak of it as having become twofold, as cut, as split, and as existing in many ways;
as lost, as to be sought, as empty, as full, and as increased. (7.83)
"It is excellent that everything is non-existent; this is the first stage, the increase of the limbs.
Speak of the one possessing accomplishment as he goes forth; one should speak of him as increased when he is asleep. (7.84)
One should not converse with barbarians, fools, the fallen, the cruel, those who revel in causing distress, the wicked, the arrogant, or the base. (7.85)
One should not dwell in a region overrun by unrighteous kings, infested with gadflies and mosquitoes, filled with excessively cold water, or one that is prone to disease. (7.86)
One should not perform sitting, lying down, drinking, salutation, or respectful greeting while wearing shoes; nor should one read the scriptures of Śiva while wearing shoes. (7.87)
The teacher, a deity, a sacred ford, water that has been stirred up, clay, curd, a banyan tree, an aśvattha tree, a kapilā cow, one who is consecrated, and the confluence of rivers. (7.88)
Having offered salutations to Śiva, whatever auspicious rites of these kinds exist here, this circumambulation has been described.
One should not wear shoes, umbrellas, garments, a purifying water-vessel, a garland, a seat, a bed, or a drink that have been used by others. (7.90)
One should avoid a seat, a bed, sandals, or a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood; likewise, one should avoid resinous exudations, but not those that are red in color.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should daily attend to the grooming of his body;
he should touch and salute a tawny cow, and provide for the welfare of cows.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who properly bestows cows, especially their products, and who also brings waste land under cultivation. (7.93)
As many thousands of years as there are leaves, flowers, stalks, roots, and fruits [of that tree], for so long is one honored in the world of Śiva.
Of cows emaciated by disease, aged, abandoned in the lonely forest, afflicted by hunger and thirst, and with their minds distraught; (7.95)
Listen to the fruit of the merit of him who, having brought grass and water to the forest, provides them with effort and offers protection. (7.96)
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage, accompanied by his wife, sons, and others,
and joined by friends and servants, he shall go to the glorious city of Śiva.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there in celestial palaces that fulfill all desires,
he shall attain liberation at the end of that period, until the time of the great dissolution.
By diligently performing the rescue of cows and Brahmins even once,
one is swiftly liberated from the five great and terrible sins.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from guile, absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness. (7.100)

The five restraints (yamas), beginning with non-violence, are proclaimed for ascetics; and the observances (niyamas), beginning with freedom from anger, are remembered as those which bring about success and growth. (7.101)
The ten-fold dharma is proclaimed as the conduct of Śiva, specifically for the sake of attaining success in Śiva-yoga by the lords of yogins. (7.102)
A man who is attached to children, wife, and the like finds no spiritual union (yoga), being bound by the snare of affection, which is strengthened by the pillar of delusion. (7.103)
Attached to family through delusion and fettered by craving, this world, bound by the foolish, is struck down with a mace. (7.104)
"How shall these fools survive without me?
For, out of delusion, he thinks in this way and does not perceive the ultimate truth. (7.105)
The insentient drop of semen, deposited in the womb through sexual union—by what effort of the father was it sustained while remaining within the embryo? (7.106)
If coarse and hard foods are digested once consumed within that very stomach, why is semen not likewise digested like food? (7.107)
By that very same [karma] by which it was joined in the womb and by which it was developed,
it emerges once more and is sustained by its own action.
No one is anyone's son, nor is anyone anyone's father or mother;
that which was one's own past karma is traditionally designated as "father" and "mother. (7.109)
Wherever and by whomsoever an action was performed, there that person is reborn;
and his parents, impelled by that same force, enter into a state of servitude.
No one is able to cause either suffering or happiness for anyone else; it is only through delusion that people believe the world acts [upon others]. (7.111)
Due to the connection of being heirs to one's karma, mutual benefit is observed rather than harm; yet, through delusion, this is imagined as being within oneself.
Action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, bears fruit here under the supervision of the Lord,
just as farming is successful through the favor of the village headman.
The duality for the sake of divinity and liberation consists of "mine" and "not mine.
By thinking "mine," a living being is bound; by thinking "not mine," one is liberated. (7.114)
The two-syllable word is death, while the three-syllable word is the eternal Brahman;
"mine" is the two-syllable word that is death, and "not mine" is the three-syllable word.
Therefore, having abandoned the sense of "I" regarding the self through discernment, and having shaken off all attachments, one should contemplate the means to liberation. (7.116)
One who seeks liberation, through wisdom, should not contemplate the hardships of yoga, nor poor clothing and food, nor bad conduct, nor a wretched dwelling. (7.117)
For all embodied beings, happiness is never seen apart from suffering; that [happiness] should be known as merely relative, while true happiness is infinite and supreme. (7.118)
When the suffering is equal in service, in cattle-herding, in trade, or in the work of agriculture, that suffering which leads to liberation is better. (7.119)
He who does not swiftly accomplish either heaven or liberation will,
upon death, long suffer with that very same body.
Since this fragile body must inevitably be abandoned by those who are subject to another's will, why does the deluded soul not strive for the eternal? (7.121)
Those kings who are in the prime of youth, those established as householders, and those dwelling in palaces—all of them alike perish, whether they consume food that is dry or succulent. (7.122)
For this body, corrupted by manifold defects, there is one great quality:
it conforms to whatever state it enters. (7.123)
Performing his work slowly, he should preserve his own body;
for like an old mat during the rains, one perishes even while remaining stationary. (7.124)
There are no embodied beings here who remain perfectly motionless;
all perform actions, weakened by their past deeds. (7.125)
Even when the duty to be performed is equal, it is better to perform the supreme action;
for one who has performed it would not again perform various actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (7.126)
Therefore, having completely abandoned internal and external thoughts established in manifold forms, one should practice self-study and meditation for the sake of one's own welfare. (7.127)
Having established a place in a secluded, solitary, and delightful spot adorned with a grove of flowers— a sacred site dedicated to Śiva— one should meditate upon the supreme Śiva, who is peaceful.
Those who abandon the most delightful forests— well-watered and auspicious—
and instead take pleasure in the village, are for the most part deluded by fate.
The bliss of one who possesses discernment, who is tranquil, and who meditates upon the auspicious, is not equaled by the bliss of Mahendra, nor of Brahmā, nor even of Keśava. (7.130)
Thus did Ṛṣyātreya obtain from Mahākāla this divine nectar of names, certain and well-ascertained, in its full detail and proper sequence.
Then, having churned the great ocean of the knowledge of Śiva with the fire-stick of wisdom, the sage Ātreya extracted this [teaching] and spoke it in its subtlest form. (7.132)
Whatever has not been stated in the *Śivadharmamahāśāstra* or in the *Śivadharma-uttara*, all that is here fully proclaimed. (7.133)
This scripture, spoken by the lord of sages, Ātreya, has three deities;
it bestows liberation upon all—animals, humans, and gods alike. (7.134)
Nandi, Skanda, and Mahākāla are proclaimed as the three gods;
Candrātreyas, Atri, and the sage Ātreya are the triad of sages.
The Śiva-dharmas have been proclaimed in brief by these great-souled ones for the benefit of all the world; salutations to them, salutations always! (7.136)
The lake of Śiva’s knowledge was pervaded by their disciples and grand-disciples, who were expounders of the Śiva-dharma, like a pond filled with blossoming lotuses.
Those who constantly cause the Śiva-dharma to be heard by those seeking Śiva are Rudras and lords of sages; they are to be honored with one's own devotion. (7.138)
Those who, having risen, listen to the Śivadharmas day after day, are Rudras, lords of the world of Rudra; they are not ordinary human beings.
Indeed, this Śivopaniṣad is remembered as consisting of seven chapters, composed by the sage of the Ātreya lineage out of a desire for the welfare [of all]. (7.140)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the conduct of Śiva, in the Śivopaniṣad.
Thus ends the Śivopaniṣad.
